name: Jagertee
description: Black tea and overproof rum with spice and citrus, served scalding in Alpine huts. Designed for people who have just come down a mountain.
funFact: Austrian law reserves the name 'Jagertee' for versions made with Inländerrum, an 80-proof Austrian rum; anywhere else in the EU it has to be sold as 'Jagatee' or 'hunter's tea'.

steps: Brew the black tea strong and keep it hot.
Warm the orange slice, cinnamon and cloves in the mug with the sugar.
Pour over the hot tea and stir until the sugar dissolves.
Add the rum last, off the heat.
Serve very hot with the spices left in.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Weißer Spritzer
description: White wine and sparkling water, half and half. Vienna's most-poured drink, and proof that the simplest spritz is still a spritz.
funFact: Order a 'G'spritzter' anywhere in Austria and this is what arrives; a 'Sommerspritzer' has more water, a 'Winterspritzer' more wine, and the vocabulary is taken seriously.

steps: Chill both the wine and the mineral water.
Pour the wine into a wine glass.
Top with the sparkling water.
Do not add ice — Austrians consider it dilution twice over.

name: Half en Half
description: Half still white wine, half Belgian sparkling, poured cold. Brussels' aperitif, and older than most of the city's cocktail bars.
funFact: It is the house pour at Brussels' oldest wine bars around the Grand-Place, where the sparkling half is traditionally a Belgian méthode traditionnelle rather than champagne.

steps: Chill both wines well.
Pour the still white wine into a wine glass.
Top with the sparkling wine, poured slowly down the side.
Serve immediately without ice or garnish.

name: Maitrank
description: White wine steeped with sweet woodruff, sugar and cognac, drunk in May with a strawberry in the glass. Arlon's own, and legally protected.
funFact: Arlon holds a Maitrank festival every May and the recipe carries a protected designation; woodruff must be picked before it flowers, or it turns bitter and mildly toxic.

steps: Wilt the woodruff for a few hours so its aroma develops, but do not let it flower.
Steep it in the white wine with the sugar and orange slices for about 24 hours in the fridge.
Strain out the herb and orange.
Stir in the cognac and chill thoroughly.
Serve in wine glasses with a strawberry in each.

name: Berliner Weisse mit Schuss
description: Berlin's sour wheat beer sweetened with raspberry or woodruff syrup, served bright red or alarming green in a wide bowl glass.
funFact: Napoleon's troops reportedly called it 'the champagne of the north'; the syrups were added in the twentieth century because the unadulterated beer was too sour for modern palates.

steps: Pour the syrup into the bottom of a wide bowl-shaped glass.
Pour the cold Berliner Weisse over it slowly — the beer foams aggressively.
Let the head settle, then top up.
Serve with a short fat straw, which is traditional and genuinely useful.

name: Feuerzangenbowle
description: A rum-soaked sugarloaf set on fire above a bowl of mulled wine, dripping caramel into it as it burns. German Christmas at its most theatrical.
funFact: The 1944 film 'Die Feuerzangenbowle' made it a national ritual; German students still hold screenings where the audience makes the drink along with the film.

steps: Heat the wine with the citrus slices and spices in a wide bowl — hot but never boiling.
Set the metal Feuerzange tongs across the bowl and place the sugarloaf on them.
Soak the sugarloaf with overproof rum and set it alight.
Keep ladling more rum over the loaf as it burns and drips caramelised sugar into the wine.
When the sugar has gone, stir the bowl and ladle into mugs.
recipe.garnish: An orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Glühwein
description: Red wine heated with cinnamon, clove and citrus. The smell of every Christmas market between Cologne and Vienna.
funFact: German law regulates it: Glühwein must be made from wine, cannot be watered down, and must not fall below 7% ABV — a rare case of a mulled drink with a legal definition.

ingredients.amount: 1 oz / 30 ml per mug, optional 'mit Schuss'

steps: Put the wine, orange slices, spices and sugar in a pan.
Heat gently to about 70°C — steaming but never simmering, or the alcohol goes.
Hold at that temperature for 20 minutes to let the spices infuse.
Strain into mugs, adding a shot of rum to each for 'mit Schuss'.
Serve hot with a cinnamon stick.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a cinnamon stick

name: Kalte Ente
description: 'Cold duck': white wine and sparkling wine over a spiral of lemon peel, chilled hard. A German garden-party punch that Americans misheard into their own version.
funFact: The name is probably a corruption of 'kalte Ende' — the cold end of the evening, when leftover wines were combined. American 'Cold Duck' took the name and made it a sweet red sparkling instead.

steps: Peel the lemons in one continuous spiral and hang the peel in a punch bowl.
Add the sugar and the juice of one lemon and stir.
Pour in the still white wine and chill for at least two hours.
Add the sparkling wine and a block of ice just before serving.
Ladle into wine glasses.

name: Lumumba
description: Hot chocolate with a shot of brandy or dark rum and a cap of whipped cream. Northern European winter, no further explanation offered.
funFact: Named — with no clear justification and a fair amount of later discomfort — after Congolese independence leader Patrice Lumumba, sometime after 1961. It is often now simply called a 'Tote Tante' in the north.

ingredients.item: Hot chocolate, made with whole milk

steps: Make a rich hot chocolate with whole milk and good dark chocolate.
Pour into a warmed mug, leaving room at the top.
Stir in the brandy or rum.
Cap with whipped cream and dust with cocoa or grated chocolate.

name: Barbajada
description: Milan's forgotten winter drink: hot chocolate, coffee and whipped cream beaten together until foamy, with a shot of liqueur if the weather warrants.
funFact: Named for Domenico Barbaja, a nineteenth-century Milanese waiter who became one of Europe's most powerful opera impresarios — he invented the drink before he discovered Rossini.

steps: Make a thick hot chocolate and keep it hot.
Combine it with the hot espresso in a jug.
Whisk in the whipped cream vigorously until the whole thing is foamy.
Add the liqueur if using, pour into a warmed mug and dust with cocoa.

name: Barracuda
description: Gold rum, Galliano and pineapple, topped with prosecco. Tropical and Italian at once, and an official IBA drink since 2011.
funFact: It is one of the newer additions to the IBA list, and one of the only official cocktails that combines a tiki structure with an Italian sparkling wine top.

steps: Shake the rum, Galliano, pineapple juice and lime juice with ice.
Strain into a large glass over fresh ice.
Top with cold prosecco.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge and a lime wheel.

name: Bicicletta
description: Campari, white wine and soda — the low-proof afternoon drink named for how its drinkers wobbled home.
funFact: Northern Italian lore says it is named for the elderly regulars who cycled home from the bar afterwards, taking a somewhat scenic route.

steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add the Campari and the white wine.
Top with a splash of soda.
Stir gently and garnish with an orange or lemon slice.

name: Caffè Corretto
description: An espresso 'corrected' with a shot of grappa or sambuca. Ordered at the bar, drunk standing, over in ninety seconds.
funFact: In some northern Italian bars you can order it 'separato' — the spirit arrives in its own glass so you can decide how much correction the coffee actually needs.

steps: Pull a fresh espresso into a warmed cup.
Add sugar if you take it, and stir.
Pour the grappa straight into the coffee.
Drink standing at the bar, immediately.

name: Milano-Torino
description: Campari and red vermouth, equal parts, over ice. The two-ingredient ancestor of the Americano and the Negroni both.
funFact: The name is geographic: Campari from Milan, Vermouth di Torino from Turin. Add soda and it becomes an Americano; add gin instead and you have a Negroni.

steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Add the Campari and the vermouth.
Stir for 15 seconds to chill and lightly dilute.
Garnish with an orange slice.

name: Rossini
description: Prosecco over fresh strawberry purée — the Bellini's red sibling from the same bar, named for the same kind of artist.
funFact: Harry's Bar in Venice named a whole family after Venetian painters and composers: peach makes a Bellini, strawberry a Rossini, pomegranate a Tintoretto, and mandarin a Puccini.

ingredients.amount: 1 barspoon, if the strawberries are tart

steps: Blend fresh strawberries and pass through a fine sieve to make a smooth purée.
Chill the purée thoroughly — a warm purée will kill the bubbles.
Pour the purée into a chilled flute.
Top slowly with prosecco, stirring gently with a barspoon as you pour.

name: Ve.n.to
description: Grappa shaken with chamomile-infused honey and lemon. Italy's own entry into the modern IBA canon, built to make grappa approachable.
funFact: The name plays on 'vento' — wind — and on the initials of the Veneto region; it was added to the IBA list in 2011 as a deliberate showcase for grappa, which had almost no cocktail presence.

steps: Infuse honey syrup with chamomile flowers by steeping them in warm syrup for 20 minutes, then strain.
Add the grappa, chamomile honey, lemon juice and apple juice to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 12 seconds.
Double-strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a chamomile flower or a lemon twist.

name: Kopstootje
description: 'Little head-butt': a tulip glass of jenever filled to the brim and a beer beside it. First sip taken bent over, hands behind your back.
glassware: Tulip glass and a beer glass
funFact: The jenever is poured to a convex meniscus, so the only way to take the first sip without spilling is to lean down to the glass — hands behind the back is the traditional form.

steps: Chill the jenever thoroughly and fill the tulip glass right to the brim.
Pour a cold pilsner alongside it.
Bend down to the jenever glass, hands behind your back, and take the first sip without lifting it.
Then pick up the glass, finish the jenever, and chase it with the beer.

name: Nikita
description: Beer, pineapple, white wine and vanilla ice cream, blended. It should be a disaster. Madeira has been proving otherwise since the eighties.
funFact: Named after the Elton John song 'Nikita', which was in the charts when a Câmara de Lobos bar owner first blended it in the mid-1980s.

steps: Put the pineapple, ice cream and white wine into a blender.
Add the beer last, to control the foam.
Blend briefly — just enough to combine, or it will overflow.
Pour into a tall glass and serve with a spoon and a straw.

name: Poncha
description: Madeiran cane spirit muddled with honey and lemon using a wooden 'caralhinho'. Sweet, sharp and much stronger than it lets on.
funFact: The stirring tool — a ridged wooden stick called a caralhinho — is specific to Madeira, and the fishermen's original version was drunk as a cold remedy before going out in the morning.

steps: Put the honey and lemon juice into a small tumbler or a jug.
Work them together with a wooden stick or muddler until the honey fully dissolves.
Add the aguardente and the orange juice if using.
Stir vigorously until frothy and serve at room temperature, without ice.

name: Porto Tónico
description: White port and tonic over ice with mint. Portugal's answer to the Gin and Tonic, and arguably the better summer drink.
funFact: Port houses pushed it hard in the 2010s to sell white port, which had been the least-loved category in the Douro — it worked so well it is now the default aperitif in Porto.

steps: Fill a large wine glass with ice.
Pour in the chilled white port.
Top with cold tonic water.
Stir once gently and garnish with a mint sprig and an orange slice.

name: Agua de Valencia
description: Cava, orange juice, gin and vodka in a jug. Tastes like a Mimosa, behaves like something else entirely.
funFact: Invented at Café Madrid in Valencia in 1959, when a group of Basque regulars kept ordering 'Agua de Bilbao' — the house sparkling wine — and the barman offered them a Valencian alternative made with local oranges.

steps: Stir the sugar into the orange juice in a large jug until dissolved.
Add the gin and vodka and stir again.
Top with cold cava and stir once, gently.
Serve immediately in wine glasses over a little ice.
Make it in front of people — half the drink is the theatre of the jug.

name: Leche de Pantera
description: 'Panther's milk': gin or rum, condensed milk and cinnamon, shaken cold. Spanish Legion issue, now a Madrid dive-bar staple.
funFact: The recipe is traditionally attributed to the Spanish Legion, whose founder Millán-Astray is said to have served it to recruits — the modern Madrid version usually swaps the original brandy for gin.

steps: Add the gin, condensed milk, milk and cinnamon to a shaker with ice.
Shake hard for 15 seconds until thick and cold.
Strain into a chilled tumbler.
Dust with more cinnamon and serve very cold.

name: Queimada
description: Orujo set alight in a clay bowl with sugar, coffee beans and lemon peel while somebody reads a spell over it. Galicia does not do this ironically.
funFact: The conxuro — the incantation read while it burns — invokes the meigas, Galician witches, and asks them to leave. The ritual is old-looking but was largely written in the 1950s.

steps: Pour the orujo into a wide clay bowl and add most of the sugar, the coffee beans and the lemon peel.
Put a ladleful of orujo and the remaining sugar into a separate ladle and set it alight.
Lower the burning ladle into the bowl to ignite the whole surface.
Stir with the ladle, lifting burning liquid and pouring it back, for several minutes until the flame turns low and blue.
Cover to extinguish, then serve hot in small clay cups.

name: Rebujito
description: Manzanilla sherry lengthened with lemon-lime soda over crushed ice — the drink that keeps Seville upright through a week of Feria.
funFact: It is drunk by the jug at the Feria de Abril in Seville and the Feria del Caballo in Jerez, where the sherry comes from — and where sherry purists have made their peace with it.

steps: Fill a tall glass with crushed ice.
Pour in the cold manzanilla.
Top with lemon-lime soda.
Stir once and add a mint sprig if you like.
Drink fast — it dies as the ice melts.

name: Sol y Sombra
description: 'Sun and shade': brandy and anís in equal parts, no ice. A Spanish breakfast that predates any conversation about moderation.
funFact: The name comes from the bullring, where seats are priced by whether they sit in sun or shade; the drink mixes the dark brandy and the clear anís the same way.

steps: Pour the brandy and the anís into a small tumbler.
Stir once to combine.
Serve at room temperature, without ice.
Traditionally taken standing at the bar, with coffee.

name: Vermut
description: Red vermouth on ice with a splash of soda, an olive and a slice of orange. Sunday noon in Barcelona has a drink and this is it.
funFact: 'Fer el vermut' — to do the vermouth — is a whole social occasion in Catalonia, held late on Sunday morning, and the best bars still draw their vermouth from the barrel.

steps: Fill a tumbler with ice.
Pour in the cold red vermouth.
Add a short splash of soda.
Stir once and garnish with an orange slice and a skewered olive.
Serve with crisps and tinned seafood, if you are doing it properly.
recipe.garnish: Orange slice and a green olive

name: Kafi Fertig
description: Coffee with schnapps, served in a stemmed glass so you can see the colour. Swiss farmhouse fuel with a colour code all its own.
funFact: In parts of central Switzerland the strength is judged by colour: it should be dark enough that a coin dropped in the glass disappears, and no darker.

steps: Put the sugar in a small stemmed glass.
Pour in the hot coffee and stir until dissolved.
Add the schnapps and stir once more.
Serve hot, in the glass, never in a cup.
